description: Mengisi waktu luang dan kekosongan jiwa
summary: Flock Around and Find Out is a project that lets anyone follow three lesser black-backed gulls on their autumn migration from Belgium to Spain and West Africa by watching, by listening, or both. NASA's Earth Information Center shares the planet mostly through images, which leaves out people who are blind or have low vision. We answer the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing EIC temperature frames with a sonification built from the birds' real GPS tracks: the warmth under each bird sets the harmony, its latitude the melody, its daily distance the rhythm, and its distance from home a low drone. Just as you can hear a kettle boil before you read a thermometer, you can hear a bird fly into warmer air before you see it on a map
details:
Flock Around and Find Out is a project that lets you follow three lesser black-backed gulls, Eric, Nico and Sanne, from their colony in Zeebrugge, Belgium, to their winter grounds and back. All three left in autumn 2024 and returned in spring 2025. Eric wintered inland in Spain, while Nico and Sanne flew to Dakhla on the West African coast, covering between 15,646 and 20,532 km each

The sound is made directly from data. We read the color of the NASA Earth Information Center temperature frame under the bird and place it on NASA's own 16-color scale, giving a warmth value from 0 (coldest) to 1 (warmest). A Python script then mapped each row of data into a pop song chord progression from departure to destination. The warmth under the bird sets the pad chords, latitude sets the flute melody (higher in the north and mirrored on the way back), daily distance sets the marimba rhythm, and distance from the colony sets the loudness of a low cello drone. A separate chapter plays ERA5 wind from 30 October 2024, Nico's longest day of 793 km across the Bay of Biscay, where wind speed sets the tempo. Each instrument is rendered as its own track, and the browser plays sound and map on one clock, so every map layer can switch its own sound on and off

The main benefit is access. NASA's Earth Information Center communicates mostly through images, which leaves out people who are blind or have low vision. Our page can be followed entirely by ear, and it also supports screen readers, full keyboard control, large high-contrast text in light and dark themes, color blind friendly palettes, written descriptions of every recording, and reduced motion.

The intended impact is to show that Earth observation data can be heard as well as seen, and to offer a pattern others can reuse. The same mapping from data to sound could play fire detections, rainfall or spacecraft paths, giving museums, classrooms and the EIC itself a way to reach audiences that images alone miss.

The project is creative in how it joins two very different datasets into one piece of music. The planet's temperature becomes the harmony, while the animal's movement becomes the melody and rhythm. We framed the idea with a simple everyday example: you can hear a kettle coming to a boil before you read a thermometer.

We considered several factors along the way. The EIC keeps only the latest two weeks of animation (30 October to 14 November 2026), so we could not match frames to the 2024–25 tracks by date. Instead we play the frames across each journey like a score, and chose frames from the same time of year as the birds' departures. We kept warmth as a relative colour value and are clear that it is not a measured temperature. We used wind for one day only, because stretching a single day's wind across a whole journey would be misleading. We cleaned the GPS data to one position every 30 minutes, removed one impossible jump, and set the tracking-gap threshold to a full day because the solar-powered tags can sleep for up to 22 hours in late autumn. We also used shared scales and one volume level for all birds so comparisons are fair

We built the data pipeline in Python (NumPy, pandas, Pillow, mido) and R (dplyr, sf), rendered the audio with FluidSynth and FFmpeg, and built the web pages with Quarto, D3 and the Web Audio API, hosted on GitHub Pages. No special hardware was needed. The whole project can be rebuilt from the original data sources with the scripts and unit tests in our public repository by running 'quarto preview --render all'
dataRefs: NASA Earth Information Center imagery: GEOS-FP Near-Surface Temperature (SVS 5147)
projectRefs: LBBG_ADULT, Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO), Belgium, Stienen et al., CC0
ERA5 hourly 100 m wind (ECMWF/Copernicus) via the Open-Meteo historical weather API
